intro: You eat every day. Breakfast before school. Lunch at a long table. A snack when you get home. Dinner with your family. Every time, someone makes a choice. What goes on the plate? What goes in the cup?

In this unit you learn the five food groups and how they fit on a plate. You learn that water is the everyday drink. You learn that no food is bad, but some foods are for every day and some are for sometimes.
By the end, you will be able to build a plate with parts, count the colors on it, listen to your body when it says hungry and full, share food fairly, and say no thank you the polite way.
bigQuestion: How do you build a plate that helps your body every day?

timeline.t: Breakfast: oatmeal with banana and a cup of milk. Three groups before school.
Lunch: count the colors on your tray. Only one? Add a fruit.
Recess is over. You are hot. Water first, from the fountain.
A new food on the plate. One small taste. Then yes or no thank you.
After school snack: an apple or a cheese stick. Chips wait for the picnic.
Dinner: half the plate is fruits and vegetables. Rice and chicken fill the rest.
Your tummy growls before lunch. That is hungry. Time to eat.
Halfway through dinner you feel done. That is full. Save the rest.
A birthday party. Cake is a sometimes food, and today is sometimes.
Ten crackers, five kids. Two each. Everyone gets some.
A trip to the farm stand. This is where the apples come from.
Plant a bean in a pot on the windowsill. Your own tiny garden.

words.d: a sweet food that grows on a plant, like an apple or a grape
a plant food like a carrot, broccoli or peas
foods like bread, rice and cereal that come from wheat or rice plants
foods like chicken, beans and eggs that help you grow
foods made from milk, like cheese and yogurt
a food you eat most days, like fruit, bread or milk
a food you have now and then, like cake or chips
how your body feels when it has had enough food

test.q: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?
test.why: The rule is half the plate.
Bread comes from wheat. It is a grain.
Yogurt is made from milk, so it is dairy.

test.q: Why eat many colors of fruits and vegetables?
choices: Each color helps your body its own way
test.why: Different colors help different parts of you, like eyes and bones.
Water has no sugar and keeps you cool.

test.q: A new food is on your plate. What do you do?
test.why: One taste is fair. It may take many tries to like it.
Chips are a sometimes food, for a picnic now and then.

test.q: Your tummy feels warm and done. What should you do?
test.why: Full means enough. Listen to your body.

test.q: Nine strawberries, three kids. A fair share is
test.why: Nine split three ways is three each.

test.q: Where does a carrot come from before the store?
test.why: Carrots grow in the ground on farms and in gardens.

write.prompt: Draw and write a lunch plate. Put a food from each of the five groups on it. Add a drink. Then tell why each food is there and which foods on your plate are everyday foods.
tips: Name all five groups: fruit, vegetable, grain, protein, dairy.
Make half the plate fruits and vegetables.
Count the colors. Try for three or more.
Pick water or milk for the drink and say why.
